subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Defence Production. In view of the present situation in the United States, will the Minister of Defence Production make a statement on the gasoline and oil situation in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The whole question of Canadian requirements of gasoline and oil is under constant review in the Department of Defence Production. It is not anticipated at the moment that the supply of petroleum products in Canada will be seriously affected by the current strikes of oil refinery workers in the United States, except the supply of aviation gasoline which is already a matter of serious concern.
This situation has resulted in a serious reduction in the production of aviation gasoline in the United States. The petroleum administration for defence, Washington, has issued its order No. 6 which temporarily
restricts the use and forces a reduction in the consumption of aviation gasoline within the United States. The order also prohibits export except under certification by PAD.
Because of the policy of close co-operation between Canada and the United States, and as United States companies and associates supply in excess of ninety per cent of all aviation gasoline consumed in Canada, it is deemed necessary that restrictions similar to those in force in the United States be placed upon the consumption of aviation gasoline in Canada in order that reduction in Canadian consumption may be in line with that in the United States. By order in council P.C. 2754 of today's date all grades of aviation gasoline have been declared an essential material under the provisions of the Defence Production Act.
Canadian oil companies have been requested to limit their deliveries of aviation grade gasoline during the 28-day period commencing May 6, 1952, to sixty-five per cent of the amount delivered during the month of April, 1952. Arrangements have been made whereby the petroleum division of the Department of Defence Production will be prepared to take under consideration cases of unreasonable hardships, such as problems that might arise in remote areas.
The departments of national defence and transport have already curtailed their flying operations. The Department of Transport, the air transport board, and the Air Industries and Transport Association of Canada are requesting aircraft operators to eliminate all non-essential flying.

subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Would the minister say whether this will affect T.C.A. schedules in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes. T.C.A. schedules have
already been curtailed; I understand that sixteen scheduled services have been eliminated already. T.C.A. is in the same position as the other aviation services, that only sixty-five per cent of the gasoline consumed during the month of April will be allocated during the month of May.

subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Can the minister say what aviation gasoline is made in Canada, and whether any steps could be taken to increase that production without incurring a very large expenditure.

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: High octane gasoline is made at Calgary in limited quantities, but about ninety per cent of our 100-octane gasoline is imported from the United States. To supply Canada a very large expenditure would have to be made; and since the trend is toward jet flying-and of course jets use low grade fuel-it is not felt that the very large investment involved is warranted at this time.

subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Can the minister say how long it will be possible to maintain even these reduced schedules?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STRIKES OF REFINERY WORKERS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: I should think we would be able to carry them on indefinitely.

speechtext:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide, amongst other things:
1.	That for the 1953 and subsequent taxation years there be substituted for the graduated rates of tax and the defence surtax that are at present applicable to the income of individuals, the following graduated rates of tax:
(a)	17 per cent of the amount taxable if the amount taxable does not exceed $1,000,
(b)	$170 plus 19 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $1,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $1,000 and does not exceed $2,000,

(c)	$360 plus 22 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $2,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $2,000 and does not exceed $4,000,
(d)	$800 plus 25 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $4,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $4,000 and does not exceed $6,000,
(e)	$1,300 plus 30 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $6,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $6,000 and does not exceed $8,000,
(f)	$1,900 plus 35 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $8,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $8,000 and does not exceed $10,000,
(g)	$2,600 plus 40 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $10,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $10,000 and does not exceed $12,000,
(h)	$3,400 plus 45 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $12,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $12,000 and does not exceed $15,000,
(i)	$4,750 plus 50 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $15,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $15,000 and does not exceed $25,000,
(j)	$9,750 plus 55 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $25,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $25,000 and does not exceed $35,000,
(k)	$15,250 plus 60 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $35,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $35,000 and does not exceed $50,000,
(l)	$24,250 plus 65 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $50,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $50,000 and does not exceed $75,000,
(m)	$40,500 plus 70 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $75,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $75,000 and does not exceed $100,000,
(n)	$58,000 plus 75 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $100,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $100,000 and does not exceed $150,000,
(o)	$95,500 plus 80 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $150,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $150,000 and does not exceed $250,000,
(p)	$175,500 plus 86 per cent of the amount by which the amount taxable exceeds $250,000 if the amount taxable exceeds $250,000.
2.	That for the 1952 taxation year the graduated rates of tax applicable to income of individuals be the average of the present rates (including defence surtax) and the rates set out in paragraph 1.
3.	That with respect to income of corporations earned on and after January 1, 1952, the present rate of tax shall be increased from 15 per cent to 20 per cent on the first $10,000 of taxable income and from 38 per cent to 50 per cent on taxable income in excess of $10,000, and that the defence surtax be repealed.
4.	That there may be deducted from the amount of income tax otherwise payable by a corporation for a taxation year in respect of income earned on and after January 1, 1952,
(a)	the amount of income tax payable to the government of a province for that taxation year in respect of income earned on and after January 1, 1952, as a result of its operations in that province, or
(b)	5 per cent of the taxable income of the corporation of that taxation year under the Income Tax Act that is earned on and after January 1, 1952, as a result of its operations in that province, whichever is less.
Income Tax Act
5.	That for the 1952 and subsequent taxation years the maximum amount in respect of medical expenses that may be deducted in computing taxable income be increased
(a)	to $2,000 in the case of a person who may at present deduct a maximum of $1,000,
(b)	to $1,500 in the case of a person who may at present deduct a maximum of $750, and
(c)	to $500 for each dependent in respect of whom a maximum of $250 may at present be deducted, subject to a maximum deduction of $2,000 by a husband and wife between them or by a person in respect of all his dependents; and that there be included in the medical expenses that may be deducted in computing taxable income those medical expenses that at present are not included by reason only that they were not incurred in the appropriate twelve-month period in which they were paid.
6.	That crown corporations that are classed as proprietary corporations in the Financial Administration Act shall pay tax on income earned on and after January 1, 1952.
7.	That the special deduction from income to a taxpayer whose principal business is the production, refining or marketing of petroleum or petroleum products or the exploring or drilling for oil or natural gas or mining or exploring for minerals, be allowed for expenses incurred in the 1955 operations on the same basis as for expenses incurred in the years 1951 to 1954.
8.	That the special deduction from income and taxes of a taxpayer whose principal business is production, refining or marketing of petroleum or drilling for petroleum be allowed for expenses incurred in respect of deep-test oil wells in 1953 operations on the same basis as for similar expenses in operations of the years 1950 to 1952.
9.	That the exemption of the income from a metalliferous or industrial mineral mine for the first three years of production now applicable to mines coming into production during the years 1946 to 1954 be extended to mines coming into production during the year 1955.
10.	That a corporation resident in Canada whose gross revenue for a taxation year ending on or after January 1, 1952 derived from the distribution to or generation for distribution to the public of electrical energy, gas or steam is more than one-half its total gross revenue for the same period shall be entitled to a deduction from the tax otherwise payable by it under the Income Tax Act to the extent necessary to reduce to 43 per cent the rate of tax payable by the corporation under that act on that part of its taxable income for that taxation year that is derived on and after January 1, 1952 from such distribution or generation.

speakeroldname: Mr. James Sinclair (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I was going to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we follow the practice we followed yesterday and have a short general discussion on the principle of the entire resolution on the first item, then on the subsequent items stick to the actual subject matter of the items under consideration.
I think perhaps I should lead off this discussion on the first item by answering some of the points raised during the first stage of this debate when the Speaker was in the chair by certain members who dealt with tax matters in the budget debate. In his remarks the other evening the minister pointed out that many excellent speeches were made during that debate but that very few of them actually related to tax matters.

Income Tax Act
So I will confine myself to those points raised in speeches which related to tax matters coming under this resolution.
The one speech which I should mention which was entirely on tax matters, and principally on the tax matters in this resolution, was the speech by the hon. member for Hamilton West, so perhaps I could start by answering the various points which she raised. If there are further technical points which may arise during the discussion on the resolution and which may need some working out, then the minister will prepare suitable replies for delivery when the bill is before the house.
On page 1555 of Hansard for April 24, the hon. member objected to the fact that in calculating the defence surtax for 1951, taxpayers were required to take 10 per cent of the amount which was the tax before deducting the credit for dividends from Canadian taxpaying corporations. The defence surtax was also calculated before the calculation of the credit for any foreign taxes. By this arrangement the tax is increased or decreased by any surcharge or payment before applying any tax credit, and this arrangement is not new. It has been the existing practice.
I shall give an example of when we reduced the tax by a percentage, the very opposite of what was done in 1951. When the tax was reduced by 4 per cent in 1945 and 16 per cent in 1946, those percentage reductions were applied before applying the tax credits for foreign taxes. Those, of course, were the only tax credits we had at that time. The hon. member will appreciate that the effect of that was to give a maximum reduction, since it was on the larger amount. The arrangement of the 1951 form carried out the intent of the 10 per cent tax credit for dividends, which was that the total tax of the taxpayer be reduced by an amount equal to 10 per cent of the net dividend income from Canadian tax paying corporations. Actually, the observation applied only to tax returns for 1951, since we have now removed the surcharge, and it is not a problem which will recur.
On page 1556 of Hansard the hon. member referred to the recommendation of the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants that the taxpayer be permitted to add dividend income of his spouse in excess of $250 to his own income and so receive the benefit of the same 10 per cent tax credit for Canadian dividends. The exemption of the taxpayer is reduced when his spouse has an income over $250 because the extent to which the taxpayer has to support his spouse is reduced if the spouse has extra income. The extent to which the
taxpayer has to support his spouse is reduced regardless of whether the spouse's income is from dividends, interest or wages. This suggested amendment would give special alleviation only to the couple where the spouse's income was from dividends.
On page 1556 of Hansard the hon. member referred to a case where the taxpayer supported a dependent sister in 1951. The taxpayer incurred heavy medical expenses in respect of this dependent sister in 1951, but was able to pay only a small part of them. Finally the dependent sister died in 1951. I think that is the situation. The member stated that the taxpayer is not allowed to claim an allowance against his 1952 tax for the medical expenses incurred and paid in the twelve-months period ending in 1952 because the sister, having died in 1951, is no longer a dependent of the taxpayer. This does not appear to be in accordance with the law. Section 26(l)(b)(iii) reads in part, "or any dependent in respect of whom he may make a deduction from income under section 25 for the year in which the expense was incurred." I am informed by the officers of the Department of National Revenue that they would like to have the details of this case from the hon. member.
May I ask a question? Do I understand the parliamentary assistant to imply that the subsequent amounts as paid will be allowed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If they are for the twelvemonths period ending in 1952, even though the sister is now deceased and is not classed as a dependent so far as the dependent exemption for this year is concerned.
That is new.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the interpretation which the officials have placed on section 26(l)(b)(iii). Once again, it is an administrative point. Perhaps if the hon. member would see the officials-

I am wondering if that is because of the amendment which was made by the minister this year in withdrawing the word "incurred". Prior to the budget speech this year, the expenses were theoretically supposed to be incurred and paid in the same year, although that practice was not pressed in the district offices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member could follow that up with the appropriate officials.
The next point was this matter about which I am quite sure we will hear a lot this afternoon, the 4 per cent medical deduction. On page 1557 of Hansard she said that the taxpayer who has medical expenses in excess
TMr. Sinclair.]

of 4 per cent of his income loses an exemption each year equal to 4 per cent of his income. Over ten years she said the total of this amount which could not be deducted could be $1,500, and this might be the factor in deciding whether or not one of his children attended university.
This is a common slip which almost everyone who is dealing with tax returns makes. It is certainly a slip I have made myself, in regarding the amount of income exempt from tax as being an actual tax saving. If in this case the 4 per cent of a man's income is $150, that means he has an income of $3,750. Presumably he has one child, since we are looking forward to a university education ten years from now. His exemption, therefore, should be $2,150 and his taxable income would be $1,600. He has to pay 17 per cent on the first $1,000 and 19 per cent on the next $600. The loss of a $150 exemption means an additional tax of $28.50. Over ten years this would amount to $285-quite a significant sum it is true, but $28.50 per year is not likely to mean the difference between university or no university.
When I made that remark I do not think I called it tax; I think I called it tax basis.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, that is quite true. Then the member criticized the estimate I used in the case for eliminating the 4 per cent on medical expenses.

I did, yes, but not as a
major objection-only as one of the minor objections.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Subsequent to that I got a letter from a citizen in Hull also expressing grave doubts about my arithmetic, so I settled down and worked out sample cases which were then checked by the department. This citizen was thoughtful enough to send copies of the letter, not only to my minister but also to the member for Eglinton and to the member for Winnipeg North Centre. I was equally thoughtful, therefore, and sent them copies of my reply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I shall be equally thoughtful and give you a reply today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am glad that so much thought has been given to the matter.
The next case is a very difficult one which I think lawyers describe by saying that hard cases make bad law. The hon. member referred to the case of an immigrant who came into the country in November, and mentioned the impact of the family allowances. There are two situations. The first situation occurs when a Canadian child is born in November. In December the child
Income Tax Act
is eligible for family allowance of $5. Because of that the parent gets the exemption of $150 for the child in receipt of family allowance-that is the lower exemption- but they have only had $5 in family allowances. However, at the end of the family allowances for eleven months at $8, making $88. Because the family allowance is not payable in the last month. The taxpayer is now eligible for the larger income tax deduction of $400, so that averages out.
This case mentioned by the hon. member, however, does not average out because the immigrant family comes in here at the end of the year, and a year later the children become qualified for family allowance. They draw family allowance for just one month, but because of that the parent, the father, on his income tax return can claim only $150 instead of $400. It is a problem which is known. There is no easy answer for it. It has been suggested that perhaps we could pro rate both the family allowance and the income tax exemption across the months. That would be a fairly difficult problem as far as administration is concerned. Since this case is so rare,-and it is rare for one reason, namely that it is a fairly fortunate immigrant who at the end of one year is in a position to be paying substantial income tax-it has been decided not to change it, or not to make it, as the hon. member suggested, optional whether they take the family allowance or not.
That leads me automatically into the other comment which was made in connection with this particular item on the impact of taxes and family allowances. I refer to the now famous speech by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I know he has been dealt with rather severely by some of his colleagues, so I will not say anything uncharitable about him; but I will deal with the proposal he makes purely from the point of view of the impact of taxation under item 1.
To be entirely fair to the hon. member I want to read his exact words as reported at page 1573 of Hansard:
The taxpayers are going to spend $332 million this year on family allowances. I say at once that most of this money will be well spent, but I cannot help wondering how badly my good friend, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), needs three family allowance cheques to make ends meet. There must be many other people in Canada in the same category.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he apply a means test to the baby bonus too?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Over my dead body.

I thank the minister for his question and I should like to answer it. I wonder whether it is sensible to pay old age pensions or family allowances to those with an income say of $5,000 a year or more. I take that figure out of the air, as perhaps it should be $6,000.

Income Tax Act
I should like hon. members to keep especially in mind that figure.
I am referring to those people who have no need of them. If the minister adopted this suggestion my closest estimate is that he would save the taxpayers about $30 million.
The hon. member was not here when the first family allowance bill was passed, so perhaps he has forgotten the implication of it. When the bill was first passed it was designed to help the lower income families, families with less than $3,000. A man who paid no income tax got the full amount, and then the benefit tapered off so that at $3,000 a man with a family really got no benefit. The extra taxes he paid and the family allowance evened out.
One year's experience with that, however, showed that it had the same grave weaknesses that our former old age pension scheme had. There were two weaknesses. The first, so far as the public was -concerned, was that this family allowance then had, in the minds of many people, the stigma of charity, the stigma of almost poverty; it was only people who were poor who were going to get it. In this country we have a great many proud people-that is, proud in the good sense of wanting their own independence-and they are not going to take handouts from anybody. During that first year a great many people who actually needed these allowances and who qualified for them would not take them because of that consideration. At the end of the first year a change was made in the Income Tax Act.
I may say that the second point-and an important point as far as the cost of government is concerned; and I know that is of great concern to the hon. member-is this. If the parent had the choice of having the family allowance and the $150 exemption or of not taking it and getting the $400 exemption, every single income tax form would then have to be checked over with the Department of National Health and Welfare to see whether the child had got the allowance. That would involve an enormous amount of paper work or red tape for both departments. Consequently a better plan was worked out the next year by the income tax department and the Department of National Health and Welfare, whereby the same result was achieved through the use of taxation but not with an open, obvious means test-with the humiliations which go with a means test and the stigma of charity which led certain proud and independent families to say: no, we will not get it-and at the same time preserving this important point that this money was not going to families such as those referred to by the hon. member.

Let me show you quickly and easily just how this plan works out. The hon. member for Moose Jaw suggested as an example this innocent bystander, the -hon, member for Comox-Albemi. I think it is most unfortunate to use as an example somebody who had not participated in the debate. As a matter of fact, I have the same view as has the income tax department, namely, that the individual's personal income is a matter for himself. However, we are extremely fortunate this week in seeing, in a national magazine, an estimate of the income of the hon. member for Moose Jaw; and since he raised the question-
Work it out on his basis.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is exactly the basis on which I want to work it out. If hon. members will just follow item 1, they will find that the income attributed to the hon. member by this magazine, which prides itself on the accuracy of its research, -comes under item (k) of resolution 1, whereby the marginal rate is 60 per cent. If we had not this new family allowance scheme, the hon. member could claim a $400 exemption for his one child, but because this family allowance is now made applicable to everybody he is allowed only $150 and receives family allowance. We have therefore removed $250 and put it back in the taxable income on this 60 per cent rate, which means he pays $150 more tax, quite aside from his other taxes, for the privilege of receiving $84 a year in family allowances. Therefore, far from having no means test and giving these family allowances to the rich, we actually are making the rich pay toward this great social measure even more than they did under the first year's plan where there was this arbitrary-, open means test.
I could describe it as having a built-in means test where there is no public humiliation, where all may recognize that whether they take it or not, they are going to be assessed as having taken it; where the people who need the benefit get the most benefit; and where those in the upper classes-in the brackets to which the hon. member referred in his speech-not only get no benefit but have to make a fairly substantial contribution toward this fund.
Hon. members might ask me now where the breaking point is. It is an interesting breaking point. The hon. member, in his innocence-I was going to say in his ignorance, but "innocence" is perhaps a nicer word, and being charitable I will use it- suggested $6,000. The average family allowance across Canada is $6; that is $72 a year. Where, on this $250 difference between the income tax exemption given for a family

allowance child and a non-family allowance child, does the tax equal that amount? At the 30 per cent level 30 per cent of $250 is $75. Again, if hon. members will just follow item 1-and I am keeping deliberately to this item

you will find that the 30 per cent level starts with taxable income of $6,000. Hence we actually achieved four or five years ago the very purpose which the hon. member set out to establish in his speech, and I think it is a purpose which everybody interested in this legislation thinks is the best way out. We have no obvious means test. It is a solution which gives the maximum benefit to the people who are most deserving of it.
Curiously enough, exactly the same built-in provision now occurs in our new old age pension plan. You might expect that. The able Minister of National Health and Welfare had this experience with family allowances; we heard for many years the objection everybody made to the open means test that is contained in the former old age pension, and with that experience in mind we were able immediately to apply a similar provision through taxation-the taxation outlined in this schedule-to the old age pension.
Once again I want to be fair to the hon. member and not put words in his mouth. I will read the exact words he used in referring to the need for a means test in connection with the old age pension. This is again to be found at page 1573 of Hansard.
He said:

McLean, now qualifies for the $40 monthly cheque, although I do not know whether he is collecting it or not.

do not know whether he takes it or not-we take $30 back, leaving him a net of $10 a month. Therefore on the year he is $120 better off because of the introduction of this means-test-free old age pension.

I would presume that a man in the bracket of a multi-millionaire would spend $10,000 a year on goods other than food, fuel and building materials; in other words, goods on which sales tax is payable. I know that the hon. member made these suggestions in good faith. He also mentioned the Prime Minister.

May I ask a

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

The next point made by the hon. member for Peace River was that the total tax load per capita in 1938-39 was $69.12, and that by 1951 this had risen to $360. A comparison of the total per capita tax payments in two separate years is not a very good indication of changes in the total tax burden. A study of the national accounts shows that the total tax take of the federal, provincial and municipal governments from the Canadian people in 1939 was over 21 per cent of the net national income. In 1951 the percentage of net national income taken by the three levels of government was about 29 per cent.
I wish to comment on that figure. This is not a large increase, in view of the enormous costs of the war and the present defence program which must be met by increased taxation. The comparison between 1938-39 and 1951 covers not only six years of the most expensive war in history, but also extensive post-war defence operations. That is the point I wish to make, so far as that 29 per cent is concerned.
Furthermore, the hon. member for Peace River overlooks the extent to which taxes are now only transfer payments going back to

Canadians in such forms as family allowances, old age pensions, and interest on the public debt, various grants and subsidies to special groups, and payments to the provinces. This would include coal subsidies, and the like. Transfer payments of this kind to the provinces-subsidies, tax rentals and the like-are not properly speaking expenditures by the federal government, since they do not spend the money.
In the analysis by the Australian economist, Clark, to which reference has been made, he places the danger point on government spending at 25 per cent. That is exclusive of transfer payments. But transfer payments by the federal government last year amounted to about $1,500 million. I think those are probably the main points raised on item 1 of the income tax resolution.

First of all I want to compliment the parliamentary assistant on the excellent presentation of these matters that he has made both today and yesterday. I hope that he can continue his good record with respect to the matter that I now want to bring to his attention. It has to do with the question of dependents allowances, and

has particular application to a subject he has just been discussing, the question of the old age pensioner. I hold in my hand a copy of the individual income tax form. This happens to be my own most recent tragic experience. I find at the top of page 2 a statement beside one of these orange asterisks, which the department likes so well, to the effect that one may not claim a dependent whose income was over $500.
I think a very unrealistic situation has arisen as a result of our no-means-test old age pension. I am sure we all realize that in every instance the old age pension is considered as income for taxation purposes. We are paying $480 a year to all our citizens 70 years of age and over with appropriate residence in Canada, but are only allowing $500, or $20 more, as a deduction for 'the children who in many instances support them. I think that is wrong. I think it is unrealistic in the light of our excellent Old Age Security Act.
There is another smaller but still very important group of people to whom I think my contention applies. I refer to people of junior age, particularly those who are attending university at the present time. The provision there respecting income is a limit of $500. There was a time in the very early twenties when the parliamentary assistant and I went to university together. It was a very rare occasion when a student could make $500 in a summer. At the present time if they are any good at all they do not have a great deal of difficulty making $500, and I think it is a good thing that they do not because universities have found that their costs have risen. In almost every instance they have had to raise their fees to a considerable extent. Today such fees are in the neighbourhood of $350 compared with the $75 that I used to pay. Having regard in the first instance to our old age pensioners and also having regard to the inflated conditions confronting our younger people today, I think we have an economic anachronism there. I have made representations on this matter to the minister already, and if he were to give it study I think he would see the justice and fairness of the claim. I hope that in the future he will correct the situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member did raise this question with the minister. It is one which normally would not come to the attention of most citizens, and I suppose most members of parliament, until next spring when the sons and daughters who are supporting their parents will suddenly realize that they can no longer claim as dependents those whom they have been claiming up until
Income Tax Act
now because they are now in receipt of the means test free old age pension and their incomes are now over $500. The Minister of National Health and Welfare raised the matter on the ministerial level with the Minister of Finance. The situation is exactly as the hon. member for Vancouver South has outlined it. Everyone 70 years of age and over is now assured of $480, and if such a person has additional income of $200 his total income is now $680 and he is no longer regarded as a dependent.
The minister has taken the matter under consideration and has decided that in view of the situation the allowance for a dependent is going to be increased from $500 to $600 from this year on. The situation of the young university student will of course be covered to an extent, or any other child under 21 who is able to earn money in summer vacation. The situation however is not quite as rough on the borderline of the $500, or $600 as it will be, as some members think. There is in the Income Tax Act section 31 (8) which provides that if a dependent has an income over $500-it will now be over $600 -that does not debar the person from being claimed as a dependent if the income is, we will say, $620 or $625. It would be very unfair if an income of $599 was included and an income of $601 was not. Therefore we have a tapering off provision over $600 with which some hon. members will be familiar.
The claiming taxpayer can add the amount of the excess over $600 to the tax he pays and list the person as a dependent. There is a very quick and obvious ceiling on that. In the case of the example I used of $200 additional income that person would be $80 over the ceiling. The point is of course as to where the limit is, above which it is not profitable to add the excess over $600 to the tax. If we take the $600 first of all at the base rate of 17 per cent, which is the rate paid by the great bulk of low income people who pay taxes, 17 per cent of $600 is $102, so up to $702 the tapering off provision applies.

I think on the whole it has been convenient to have this reply by the parliamentary assistant to the taxation questions that were asked. Perhaps it makes it a little difficult to go back and discuss more general considerations which I think should be discussed at this point in our study of the resolution, but nevertheless I wish to do so for a brief period of time. I hope I am not one of those people who like to go on repeating things over and over again, but I think our position with [DOT]espect to taxation at the present time is

Income Tax Act
something that should be dwelt on, that it is tremendously in the people's minds, and that now that the budget is nearly through we are going to be in great danger of getting into a situation like the weather. Everybody talks about it and nobody does anything.
Yesterday afternoon we talked for a few hours and in the course of the discussion passed resolutions covering about a billion and a half dollars. Today, if my arithmetic is good, when this resolution has been finished we will have passed a resolution covering approximately two and a half billion dollars. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should like to answer some of the points made. First, on this matter of consideration, there is no group of issues coming before the Canadian people in which every Canadian has so much interest as in taxes. I say that the Minister of Finance is quite right in saying that he will give consideration to any reasonable proposal put forward by any group in this country, from the House of Commons down to the smallest village council and on down to the smallest wage earner in this country.
All I suggested was that the House of Commons might have a special position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I myself as a member of parliament want no more special position for representations on taxes than any of my constituents.
The second point concerns this matter of consideration, because the Minister of Finance is bound, and should be bound, to give consideration to all tax proposals. These motions that are moved by private members on material matters, and which start by saying

that consideration should be given to something, have a very special implication for the minister. It was for that reason the minister instructed me to say, as I did, that of course we would give consideration to this or any other proposal. When the hon. member, at the conclusion of his remarks, tried to imply by speaking very smoothly, as he generally does, that the house was giving assent to the proposal I jumped up and said, "No, no, we are recommending that the government should consider this proposal."
I want to say that in future, so far as the present Minister of Finance is concerned, if such proposals are going to be moved immediately before the budget, while the minister will give them consideration, they are not to be accepted in that sense. Obviously, if acceptance of a motion for consideration before the presentation of the budget means acceptance of the principle, then the whole principle of budget secrecy is gone. Every member would load down the order paper with every conceivable resolution on every phase of the tax structure.

You are
really admitting my whole point. Thank you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the parliamentary assistant permit a question on that point? Would he explain why that attitude is being taken with respect to a motion this year referring to the deductibility of medical expenses, when a year ago a motion respecting the deductibility of trade union dues was not accepted but was voted down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Obviously that was the right thing to do, and for the very reason I have been advancing, because in the end the thing was done.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, the government does the opposite of what the house votes for. Is that it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
What I was trying to point out was that, far from the government doing the opposite of what the house has voted for, if hon. members want to load down the order paper before the budget with every conceivable resolution on tax matters, and once the government said they would accept them for consideration it meant they were inevitably in the budget, then we would be in the position of having no budget secrecy. Under the British parliamentary system, budget secrecy is important so that no group shall have undue advantage by knowing of budget changes.
The second point is even more interesting, because if there was one thing I thought the hon. member for Greenwood would have

understood with his long experience in business, it was that the government is anxious to bring about as little disturbance in industry in this country, and to avoid as much unnecessary paper work as possible. In my budget speech I explained at some length the reason why we have this division in the middle of the year. It has nothing to do with the government. In the old days when income tax was paid in a lump sum in the spring, no such problem arose. Today, when we deduct the great bulk of income tax through payroll deductions, week by week or fortnightly or monthly, depending upon the way the employee is paid, we have to supply every employer in the country with a tax schedule to show at what rate he should make deductions from his employees, dependent first of all on their wage and secondly their marital status. These deductions are incorporated in every pay sheet for every industry in this country.
If we were, for example, to have incorporated the full 20 per cent surcharge in last year's taxes, it would have meant that we would have had a 40 per cent surcharge for the last six months of the year because the budget was not approved until June. Then, immediately after January 1 of this year, the surcharge would have been returned to the 20 per cent, because it would have been for the whole year. This would have meant a double change in the tax schedules and payrolls of industry. It is for that reason that every tax change we have had since we adopted this policy of deductions at source- a policy which is not only convenient to government but is a real convenience so far as the individual taxpayer is concerned because he does not have to find a large sum in the springtime-has resulted in this split in the year's taxation.
Last year, for example, the tax tables which were in effect for the first half of the year were the tax tables without the surcharge which was only approved and given the royal assent in June. During the second half of the year the 20 per cent surcharge went into effect, so the same schedule could be used this year if no tax changes were made. Those schedules are in effect now. We hope that the income tax bill will be approved and become law by June, so that on July 1 the new rates which are mentioned here can be incorporated. For the first half of this year, the deductions will have been made at the 20 per cent surcharge level.

All I am
saying is that by chopping and changing you make it difficult.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is a little different from the inference given. Now that I have explained that it is a convenience to both the taxpayer and industry, the hon. member is backing away from it.

I was going to say that, first of all, the parliamentary assistant has just said that a vote on a private member's resolution should be treated by the government in a manner different from a vote on a government measure. I have always felt that members of the house should be free to vote as they wish on a private member's resolution. This afternoon the parliamentary assistant made a statement that the government in the future will have to see that resolutions of the description of the one which we were discussing will not be approved by the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: On tax matters before the budget.

Yes, on tax matters by the government. I take it that is the decision of the government for future guidance. I think that is unfortunate. I think that, on occasion, we should have in the House of Commons opportunities for members of the house to vote freely. I know that I was criticized for a statement made in the same connection outside the house and repeated in the house.
I know that some members felt that I had been rather harsh in what I had said. But the statement made by the parliamentary assistant this afternoon would give colour and credence to what I said.
I think that there are two different sorts of resolution which come before the house.
I understand perfectly well that when the government brings down a motion in support of a policy which has been decided upon by the cabinet and has been thoroughly discussed by them, they expect their own members to support it. That is one thing. But when we have before the house a private member's resolution simply asking the government to consider something, I think that every hon. member should have the opportunity and the right to vote as he pleases in that connection, asking the government to consider something.
I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that the wording of such a resolution does not bind anybody. But there are no opportunities for members of the house to express themselves as a house, apart from party allegiances, if we consider a resolution moved by a private member, particularly from the opposition side of the house, to be one that the government members must of necessity vote down. I think that is an unfortunate position into which we are getting in this parliament and, as a matter of

Income Tax Act
fact, in other parliaments as well. X dislike the congressional system in the United States where the party lines are somewhat more flexible, but in the interests of the expression of the opinion and the will of private members, I think that we in this house should give some thought to our particular problem.
I am glad that the parliamentary assistant dealt with the question of a means test; and I think he did it extremely well. I think he *confirms the opinion that most of us in this chamber hold, namely that the means test should have been abolished earlier; and we were happy when it was abolished. As I interjected, I think that the position would have been greatly strengthened if, in the 2-2-2 formula the government had not placed the ceiling of the $60 maximum payment by income taxpayers. It would then have been based more on ability to pay than it was. But on the whole, I think that the explanation he gave today is one that is acceptable to the committee.
I want to add this. I do not care where you attempt to put the means test, you are going to have two difficulties arise. You are going to make the people who come under the means test and get the pension feel that they are accepting something of a semicharitable nature. That illustrates one of the great advantages of abolishing it. The other thing is this. I think most of us in the committee know that a few people who normally were fairly honest sometimes stretched their consciences a little far in making application for the old age pension. I am indeed glad that no one is now compelled or invited to stretch his conscience. In dealing with taxation matters I think we should encourage our people to be honest in every respect and that we should see to it that nothing in the nature of deception is invited or permitted in connection with our income and other taxes. I believe that the government and the officials of the department have been trying to do this in all particulars.
What I really rose to say is this. The income tax is of course the fairest form of taxation. It is based primarily on ability to pay; and as we have it in this country, it is on a graduated plan. I believe, however, that it is a pity that the government did not consider raising the exemptions somewhat. The cost of living is extremely high in this country and the exemption of $1,000 and $2,000, which seemed satisfactory a few years ago, is no longer satisfactory on account of the high cost of living. I wish the government had considered raising the exemptions say to $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 or even
[Mr. Coldwell.l
$2,500 for married couples, in that way enabling a good many people to meet the increased cost of living more easily.
May I also add this thought. I do not know what the future holds, nor does any other member of this committee. But the very fact that the government felt constrained to reduce or remove the excise tax to the extent it did and to remove credit restrictions a short time ago, I think indicates clearly that there is some necessity for enabling people to buy more of the goods that are being produced. I do not want to go into this matter at all fully this afternoon because I do not believe this is the place to do it. But I want to remark that, from the study I have given to the recent trends economically, it would seem that our tremendously increased capacity for production, for turning out vastly increased numbers of goods-coupled with the fact that the Korean war perhaps has not meant that we have to produce as much in the way of war supplies as the nations thought they would have to produce and so on-is causing a piling up of goods and inventories, and people are unable to buy the goods. At such a time I think an argument can be made- and a good one-for increasing purchasing power, particularly in the lower groups, in order that they may relieve industry of some of the goods that industry is producing. I want to leave that thought with hon. members and with the government.
The other comment I want to make is this. A slight easement has been made in the corporation tax. I know that in this chamber from time to time a great deal of discussion has occurred regarding the corporation income tax. I know that from time to time the Minister of Finance and others have pointed out that our corporation income tax-particularly when you reckon in what has been done in two of the provinces-is a high tax. Indeed, it is sometimes said that it is one of the highest in the world. When we compare our corporation tax with that of the United States, for example, what I think we are overlooking, is that in the United States they have two other taxes that go with it. They have the excess profits tax, which has also been reintroduced in Great Britain. They also have a capital gains tax. As hon. members know and as you, Mr. Chairman, know, we believe there should be a capital gains tax in Canada.
At noon today, and quite at random, I happened to pick up a book on my desk and to open it at a page where certain facts were given in connection with capital gains in the United States. Here is one example that I saw. It is an outstanding one, I admit,

and not an average one but it stuck in my memory. Two hundred shares at $6 a share of the Pepsi-Cola Company in 1939 were, in 1945, worth $225,000. There is a capital gain of an extraordinary size. It seems to me that that capital gain should be taxed. The same is true of lesser capital gains where the individual does not turn a hand to do something to improve the economy of the country but takes advantage of the times in which we live. I could hardly credit that amount, but it was in a standard work on my desk today. Of course it may have been something in the nature of a misprint. There may have been a cipher in the wrong place or something or that sort. While that may not be a typical example to give, let me say this. Capital gains of enormous amounts have been made in the past few years on the stock market, in the increase in the value of land, the community creating the value of land, as Henry George used to teach us years ago. And certainly when the community creates a value it should get something from that value. We should have a capital gains tax. As for the corporation tax in our country, it is high, yes, but when we consider that other countries have an excess profits tax and a capital gains tax as well, as in the United States, then of course it does not seem as relatively high as it otherwise might do.
On the whole I want to say that in our opinion the direct form of taxation, that is, the income tax on a graduated scale, along the lines we have here-although I might, as I said, suggest a higher exemption; we might suggest too a steeper tax in certain of the brackets-is to be preferred to any other form of taxation that we know, because it is based to some extent on ability to pay.

What I would like in the future, when the government is looking for new sources of revenue and reconsidering the income tax, in view of the necessity of having as much purchasing power in the hands of the lower income groups as possible, is to see the exemption raised. It will be noticed that I said "in the lower brackets", not in the higher brackets. I think they have enough purchasing power now. The corporation income tax should also be rounded out by a capital gains tax and excess profit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: People with that amount of income are not easily disturbed. They do not have the worries that most of us have. The hon. member referred to the slight easement in the corporation tax. Some who are taxed may not get any old age pension.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is a tax on everybody; that is right. But in the end the individual presumes he will be in receipt of the old age pension if he lives that long. No matter how long the corporation lives it will not receive old age pension, so the actual practical effect as far as this is concerned is that we have given this abatement of -6 per cent in the corporation tax level, but the actual final effect of that in Canada today is that the corporations pay 52 per cent in eight provinces and 54 per cent in the other two provinces.
They just pass it on to the individuals in prices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It depends. No absolute statement of that kind can be made. It depends entirely on the competitive position of the corporation.
Corporations get subsidies and subventions, though.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Corporations are not alone in that, as my hon. friend knows. They are not alone in this matter of getting subsidies and subventions from the government. I think a considerable number of individuals across this country get subsidies and subventions in one way or another, and I think I can recall the hon. member not so long ago asking for an increase in the coal subvention.
I will likely continue that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not think the matter of a capital gains tax need be discussed again. We had a full discussion on it last year. I think most people agree that in an established society in view of the accretion in value which comes because of community effort, the sort of thing which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said was one of the principal tenets of Henry George's single tax, there is a good case for the capital gains tax. But in a pioneering country where so much of our capital is venture capital, -where it is true the amount made may be large but where a man runs the risk of losing not just his income but his capital- there is not the same case for a capital gains tax. I hear someone behind me say, "hear, hear." What I have said refers particularly to venture enterprises such as oil and mining, and enterprises generally in the northern part of this country.
The hon. member mentioned the unique case, the fantastic case, of the increase in value of the shares of a soft drink company. An increase like that is a surprising thing. So surprising is it that there must be some special reason for it. It has been suggested to me that at the time that the stock was almost worthless they were involved in a very difficult patent suit with their main competitor. Had that patent suit been lost even the $1,200 would have been down the drain. That is a very unusual case. At that time they actually ran the risk of losing their entire capital. I think these are the main points.

The parliamentary assistant has mentioned the deductions allowed for children. My understanding is that in the case of a son or daughter attending university there is an allowance of $400, if that young person is under 21 years of age.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.

Apparently there is also some administrative provision under which such university student may go out during summer months and earn up to $500 in any one year, without the father losing the right to claim the deduction of $400. As the parliamentary assistant knows, it now costs at least $1,000 a year for a student to attend a university; and it seems to me there should be some change in the administrative provision whereby the student would be allowed to earn more than $500 during the summer months.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

Is that in the budget, under the act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is done by regulation under the definition of dependency. When the minister has the bill before the house he will explain it at greater length. Because of that factor, and primarily because of the old age pension factor to which reference was made, the allowance has been raised from $500 to $600. There is a provision in the act, called the notch provision, whereby there is a tapering off when income is earned in excess of $600.

Would it not be fair to place that figure at the actual cost to the student per year? I do not think there can be any question that the cost runs to at least $1,000 a year, or perhaps more than that in some faculties-engineering and medical, for instance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That comes down to the point we discussed before, namely that of special exemptions for special groups. It is quite true that every encouragement should be given to students who want to attend university. But then there are other classes of dependents who are equally deserving, and there would be resentment if special consideration were given to university students, and not given to these other classes. It was thought that the extension of the earning power was the fairest procedure- fixing it at $600, and tapering off to $702, I believe it is. This gives leeway for extra earnings in the summer months.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I feel the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has done a real service today in the analysis he has given of the relationship between the income tax on the one hand and old age pensions and
Income Tax Act
family allowances on the other. All of us who were members of the old age security committee of 1950 will agree that it was the desire of that committee that, whatever financial arrangements were made, with the removal of the means test those in the upper income brackets would not benefit from it, but rather would pay back more than they actually received.
Most of us have known right along that that is the way it works out, and that fact is realized by most people. However there are a few throughout the country who are at times disturbed by the thought that we are using moneys of the taxpayers to make social security payments to rich people who do not need them. As I say, I believe the parliamentary assistant has performed a service today in setting out, as he did, figures to show the precise situation, which is that the wealthy pay back in taxation more than they receive in social security, and that is as it should be.
There can be no doubt that, with the exception of some modifications we might like to make-and I have in mind the $60 ceiling- the general principle of the relationship between income tax on the one hand, and old age pensions and family allowances on the other, is good. Indeed I hope the excellent statement in the matter made today by the parliamentary assistant might be read by those administering the Old Age Assistance Act, and also by members of the veterans affairs committee. We still have a couple of means tests affecting very important legislation, and I suggest that the request made by some of us from time to time for the removal of those means tests, is not wild-eyed at all, particularly in the light of the statement made this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant. It is time these other means tests were likewise abolished.
While I agree fully with what he said in that field, there was one section of his remarks with which I disagreed-and I am sure that fact will come as no surprise to him. I refer to what he had to say concerning the deductibility of medical expenses. Like my leader, I feel it is most unfortunate that the parliamentary assistant said what he did this afternoon. He has served notice, in advance, that any future private members' motions dealing with taxation matters presented in the house prior to the date of the budget will be defeated.
We have been told that there is no cracking of the whip on the government side. Well,

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member? Private members have never had any right to make decisions on taxation matters. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: When I spoke on this question on April 23 I agreed with the position of the minister as the parliamentary assistant has put it now, but I also pointed out to him that the very same sections of the rule books which confine that right to the government also spell out the right of private members to bring in motions expressing opinions on matters that should be considered. The action of the parliamentary assistant today, which has been taken in the name of the Minister of Finance, is denying us the right to get a vote on a motion expressing an opinion. I submit that the parliamentary assistant is perfectly right in telling us what the position of the government is with relation to a matter like this, but I submit we are right in pointing out what the position of private members is as a result of the announcement the parliamentary assistant has made today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I quite agree with the position now taken. In every debate on tax matters that takes place before the budget, and in the course of which consideration is asked, every member of the house can put forward his view. Whether the motion for consideration is accepted, talked out or voted down, the government is then aware of hon. members' views on tax matters because they have been able to express them publicly, but they have never had any right of decision. Let me give you a personal case quite aside from the case which I stated on behalf of the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What is it, margarine?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, I am talking again on the 4 per cent. The hon. member has referred

I felt then and still feel that in putting forward such resolutions it would be helpful to have votes to show the opinion of members, but these tax considerations are in a very different category. With respect to the hon. member's motion to give consideration, he and other hon. members have repeatedly said that the house was unanimously in favour of the principle. I voted to give consideration, but anybody reading my speech of that day or who has heard me since will realize that I do not believe in exemptions of normal expenses, whether they be medical expenses or other things. What I am doing here is saying that we are going to revert to the practice which the hon. member mentioned in discussion of his resolution concerning the deductibility of trade union dues. It was the only one I could find in my limited research on these matters, and it is the best illustration I can give. It is quite true that we had a long discussion. Various members put forward their points of view. In the end the motion was defeated but the points of view expressed by members that day did have weight with the government. However, the government did not indicate that day whether or not they were going to do it any more than the Minister of Finance gives any other indication before the budget of what action he is going to take.
When the budget was brought down it showed that not only had consideration been given despite the vote in the house, which meant nothing, but favourable consideration had been given. In future exactly the same thing will be done with respect to the very narrow group of private members' resolutions which are introduced before the budget. However, if the acceptance of such motions for consideration were to be interpreted as meaning that the wish of the house had to be implemented by the government it would lead to budget changes being disclosed in advance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before the parliamentary
assistant interjected this last time I had just asked him to see our point of view as private members of the house contrasted with the point of view of the government. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, the opportunity to air my views and the opportunity for other members to air their views in the house so the government could hear them.

speechtext: Order. It seems quite clear that the two hon. members who are now speaking are not going to agree with respect to the treatment that might be given to the consideration of private members' resolutions in the future. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am prepared to accept your ruling. Obviously each of us could go on for a considerable length of time, and it is also obvious that neither of us is going to convince the other.

speechtext: It has happened in the past.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to interject at this point? I understand he is going to leave the particular line of thought he has been following.

speechtext:
Order. If the hon. member wishes to continue the discussion of this matter he is out of order. He should not speak on it. Sufficient debate has taken place on this question which was referred to in a very incidental manner by the parliamentary assistant and taken up by the hon.

Income Tax Act
member for Winnipeg North Centre. If we are going to discuss it, then let us put aside the Income Tax Act resolution. What I have before me is the Income Tax Act resolution. I would ask hon. members to be reasonable and discuss the resolution.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I will accept your ruling. I was going to discuss the principle of the matter that the two hon. members were discussing. I think I had a better speech than either of them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member may save it for another occasion.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I get back to the resolution now before us and to a point which the parliamentary assistant discussed in his opening remarks this afternoon. When the parliamentary assistant referred to the matter this afternoon I told him that I would kindly oblige by answering one of the points he tried to make in this letter. He was good enough to send me a copy of the letter, and I should now like-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If I may rise on a point of order, we have had a pretty general discussion entirely on item 5. Could we try to make a little progress? I also have material on item 5 and I suggest that we might confine ourselves to it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am prepared to agree. I seem to be having as much trouble as the hon. member for Greenwood.

Oh no, you
are not. You are being allowed to go on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There need not be any ruling, Mr. Chairman. I accept the suggestion as being quite reasonable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: But I would ask the hon. members if the discussion on paragraph 1 has terminated.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Oh, no. Without prejudice to the right of hon. members who still wish to engage in such general discussion as you will permit, I will defer any further discussion of the medical expense question until we reach paragraph 5 of the resolution now before us.
With specific reference to paragraph 1, I was pleased with something else the parliamentary assistant did this afternoon. It happens to be in line with something I intended
[The Chairman.]
to do myself; and even at the risk of repeating what he did I think I will still do it, for a reason I shall make clear. During the course of the main budget debate a number of us complained because the Minister of Finance gave the impression that there was a decrease in taxation involved in the rates now before us as compared with the rates of last year. That is not so; there has been an actual increase, even before one adds the social security tax. The parliamentary assistant was perfectly correct in what he said this afternoon, namely that if you closely examined the words used by the Minister of Finance on the night of April 8, what he said was that the rates of taxation for 1952 following these budget changes would be a little less than they would have been had there been no change. But he has also admitted this afternoon that the rates to be paid for 1952 are actually higher than the rates for 1951.
As the parliamentary assistant knows, when the Minister of Finance delivered his budget speech he followed his usual custom and put on Hansard three sets of tables showing what the income tax payments would be. Those tables are found at page 1254 of Hansard for April 8, 1952. I draw attention to the fact that the first column in each of these tables is headed "Income"; the next column is headed "Tax for 1952 at present rates"; the next column reads, "Tax in full year at new rates" and then there is a column dealing with percentages and a final column showing the tax in 1952, with six months at the present rates and six months at the new rates. What is missing from all these tables on page 1254 is a column showing the actual tax for 1951. I have taken the trouble-like the parliamentary assistant I like to go back and see what appears in Hansard of bygone years-to go back over quite a number of budget speeches, and I have quite a collection of them here on my desk. I find that every year the present minister has presented a budget involving any income tax changes, with one understandable exception, in his tables he has given the actual tax paid the year before and the tax to be paid during the current year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If I may help the hon. member, the tables I put on Hansard at the request of the hon. member for Peace River cover this whole field.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I recognize that. I said a moment ago the hon. gentleman had done something I had planned to do, and I was glad we were thinking along the same lines.
Why do it again?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
An hon. member asks, "Why do it again?" The reason is that we have

different points of view about these matters. I have not yet seen those tables, and I want to make sure there is on Hansard a statement comparable to the kind of statement the minister has made before, showing these taxation changes from the perspective from which we see them, a perspective which I think is shared by people generally.
I was about to point out that on April 10, 1951, when taxation changes were made, the columns included the 1950 tax, the 1951 tax, the increase in 1951, and the increase in a whole year. There were no income tax changes in 1950, but if you go back to 1949 you will find the comparable tables at pages 1796 and 1797 of Hansard for March 22 of that year. In that instance there were reductions in taxation. Again the first column shows the income, the next column is the 1948 tax, the next column is the 1949 tax, and the last two columns are the reductions, first in dollars and then in percentages.
My point is that it has been the normal practice of the Minister of Finance to bring the tables before the house in that form: these were the amounts paid last year; these are the amounts which will be paid this year. But when he presented his budget on the night of April 8 this year he chose to depart from that practice. Instead of giving us the amounts that were paid last year and the amounts that will be paid this year, which would show the increase Canadians must pay, he gave as the first column the amounts that would have been paid this year under rates not being charged for this year, so that for a little while that evening he could make the suggestion of a slight decrease in taxation.
I took the trouble to work out a table, and I believe it will compare with one of the tables the parliamentary assistant has placed on the record. The hon. gentleman has now sent across to me some carbon copies of those tables. Naturally, since I am on my feet I have not had time to make a close comparison; but I would suggest-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Just read the headings, and you will find they are exactly as you suggested.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I would suggest that the table I prepared and which I would like to put on the record is simpler, in that it is only one table. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I want to raise this point, Mr. Chairman. At the request of the hon. member for Peace River-which request could have been made by the hon. member for 55704-131J

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
