Agreed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: May I make one interjection at this point? The hon. member probably recalls the very wise observation of the member for Peace River that, so far as the taxpayer is concerned, it is not the percentage increase or decrease but it is the dollar increase or decrease that is important. I think your table should include that as well.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I was trying to keep my table simple. The parliamentary assistant has put on the record tables that are complicated enough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Simply to prove your point, but not the other points. My tables are complete enough to prove anything you wish to draw from them.
We had better stop right now, then.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As a matter of fact, after I had worked out these tables-I did them in pen and ink-I thought of the very point to which the parliamentary assistant has referred. I worked those figures out, too, in pencil, but I decided-and I am not at all reluctant to give some examples, if they are wanted-that it would complicate the picture to put in another column.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Complicate your argument.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Not at all, because as the member for Cape Breton South has said, it is not the dollars you pay but the dollars you have left that count. It is one thing for the parliamentary assistant to say, if he had a chance to look at the pencilled figures on my table, that at the top bracket of $400,000 the increase is $16,073, whereas down in the lower brackets the increase may be only $7 or $13 or $17, but it is a lot easier for a person with $400,000 to pay that much of an increase than it is for some of those in the lower brackets to pay even a few dollars increase. It is not what you pay out, but what you have left that counts. A system of increases that become less in percentage as you get up into the higher brackets is contrary to the accepted practice in the field of taxation, where we believe in taxing according to ability to pay.
I agree that the government can be handed a little compliment once in a while for some things that it does. I have always been interested in the relationship between that portion of our taxes that are collected by the direct method and that portion collected by the indirect method. I am one of those who has been complaining across the years against the high proportion being collected by the sales tax and other indirect methods. I keep studying the figures and the fact is-I am free to admit it and compliment the government on it so far as it has gone-that the government has moved in the direction of a higher percentage from direct taxation and a smaller percentage from indirect taxation. If the government is acceding to some of our requests in that connection, I do not think it should hold back when it comes to the progressive nature of the income tax.
As I say, the figures I have given show that the percentage increase in the upper brackets is less than the percentage increase in the lower brackets. I have not even tried to work out what the picture is with respect to those who formerly were paying over 100 per cent. Such a calculation becomes very complicated. The parliamentary assistant knows that one of the reasons for incorporating the former defence surtax into the general income tax was to avoid that situation, so with respect to those who formerly had to pay slightly over 100 per cent their tax liability has been reduced. The highest rate in the new schedule is 86 per cent, plus 4 per cent surtax on investment income. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant knows offhand what top rate that could produce.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It could produce 90 per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Whereas formerly one could be required to pay 100 8 per cent on a top bracket.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You are certainly wanting your pound of flesh now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Pound of flesh nothing; what you have got here is an admission that there will be some people who will have an actual reduction in the amount of taxes that they will pay. They are in the very high brackets, but it is an actual reduction in terms of the percentages which the parliamentary assistant and I have agreed to be the case. Down in the lower bracket, however, the percentage increase is higher than it is in the upper brackets. I recognize that perhaps the amount of money to be obtained by adding a few per cent to the top bracket is not great, but I contend that in principle our income tax should be progressive right down the line. I object to the failure of the government to follow that course with regard to the taxation of those in the upper brackets.
I have made this speech a lot longer than I intended, mainly because of the difficulty I had over those tables, but at least I hope we have it clear now, in plain language that the man in the street can understand, that the income tax to be paid by Canadians for the year 1952 is greater than the income tax paid by Canadians for 1951.

May I speak on a point of privilege? This afternoon when I mentioned a certain figure I saw great surprise on the countenances of some members in the house. I ran up to my office to see if my memory had played tricks on me. I have before me a book entitled "The Nature and Tax Treatment of Capital Gains and Losses", by Lawrence H. Seltzer, published by the national bureau of economic research in the United States. The statement to which I referred is this:
A man who bought 200 shares of Pepsi-Cola Company common stock at $6 a share in 1939 could sell his holdings for more than $225,000 in 1945.
I appreciate the explanation that the parliamentary assistant made, but let me point out that in this case a man bought these in 1939 and sold them in 1945. An investment of $1,200 would yield a return of $225,000.
Nobody had the money to buy them then.

Somebody had $1,200 and bought them. I could cite a number of other examples, but since that is the only one I mentioned, and I thought my memory could have played tricks on me, 1 should make sure it was put accurately.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Since we are speaking to points of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I have one. When the hon. member for Greenwood was speaking about the 4 per cent floor on medical expenses, I interrupted to say that
Income Tax Act
he was repeating what he said in his speech on the budget. Since then I have re-read his speech and find that he did not mention this subject. I wish, therefore, to withdraw what I said and apologize to the hon. member.

This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra raised the question of exemptions for dependents, but I did not think he developed it as fully as it might be developed. That is with regard to the exemption for children who are dependent and who are over the age of 21. As the act now stands, in order to get an exemption a child must be wholly dependent on the parent and under 21 years of age or 21 years of age or over and dependent by reason of mental or physical infirmity. It is quite obvious that under 21 the exemption is given because of the dependence of the child upon the parent. As regards the taxpayer, what is the difference whether the child is 21 or 22? The taxpayer is penalized if the child is not mentally or physically incapacitated but is a student at a university, and is costing the parent $1,000 or $1,500 a year.
I suggest that times have changed since this exemption was put at 21. I do not know what the origin of it was or why it was put at 21. I do not know whether it was because the child was supposed to become a man or woman at 21 and therefore ought to be working. If he is working, he is not dependent. But as long as he is dependent I think there should be an allowance especially with regard to university students.
Since the war and up until the past year it was difficult for a young man coming out of high school with matriculation to get into a university. I know of one young man who had to wait and take a degree at another university before he was allowed to go into medicine. The result is that he entered the medicine course at 24. He is dependent on his parents. It is true that he will be able to get some employment during the summer months but the amount that he would earn would be far from sufficient to take him through during the rest of the year.
The same thing applies not only to medicine but to engineering and to dentistry. In the universities today we have a pre-dental course, a pre-engineering course and a premedical course. By the time a young man can graduate in engineering, he is at least 23 or 24 years of age, and he is probably older than that before he can graduate in dentistry or medicine. I was speaking to a university man today and I asked him how old the students were in first-year dentistry; and I mean the regular course in dentistry.

Income Tax Act
not the pre-dentistry course. He said that he was 25. I said: You must be much older than others. He said: No, not at all; most of them are about my age and some of them are as old as 30 or 32. As we know, a good many men came back from the war and entered on the financial arrangements provided by the government. They were, of course, much older students and they created such a demand for space in the universities that ordinary persons had to wait for two or three years.
It seems to me that it should be defined, at any rate, why is it that a person is regarded as a dependent until he is 21 but, as soon as he strikes this magic age of 21, is no longer a dependent and the taxpayer is no longer entitled to claim an exemption for him.
I have had a family of my own. Several of them have gone to university. One of them is attending the conservatory of music, which is not exactly a university. So I know what all this means. A person when studying music or medicine has no opportunity, as have other students, of earning money during the summertime to assist in financing him at university or in whatever course he is taking. I therefore feel that the government should give consideration to this matter.
I have heard parents ask about the matter. They have said to me: Why can you not get the Minister of Finance to make some exemption for our children over 21 who are attending university? They are really a dead weight or a dead load just at that particular time. If they were earning money, no parent would think of asking for that exemption. They could not anyway, because the law would not allow them to do so. I suggest that the Minister of Finance should give serious consideration to enlarging the exemption for students who are at university.

Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting for two hours to catch your eye. I am very glad that at last I, in this inconspicuous corner of the chamber, have succeeded in doing so. I was going to say a few words on the question of increased exemption but as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his speech has expressed the views of this group and the views of all of the members of the C.C.F. in Canada and of the millions of people who support those views, I shall not repeat them. I want to take the opportunity presented by this general item to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant what I consider to be a measure of injustice and to ask him a question or two. I must say that I love asking the parliamentary assistant questions. I must also say that he is extremely courteous

and usually goes to considerable trouble to answer questions asked of him verbally or when they are submitted in writing, and I appreciate that fact.
There is in my constituency a situation which no doubt is duplicated in many other places in Canada. I am now using my own personal experience or that of my constituents in order to illustrate my point. I am speaking again of the employees of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company who work in a defence industry and who, in many cases, have to travel up to 40 miles a day to and from their work. They are obliged to travel that distance in order to find accommodation for living, home sites and so on. Their services are necessary to the company and to the defence industry. That travel costs those employees from $10 to $20 a month in the way of out-of-pocket expenses depending on the distance. Those are expenses which they cannot avoid.
As I see it, Mr. Chairman, the working man or the salaried worker who has to accept a payroll deduction and the farmer who sells his crop through a marketing agency are the only persons from whom the government can be quite certain of collecting all the taxes that are due. In this connection I might point out that while these men at the present time are denied the opportunity to deduct these necessary and unavoidable travelling expenses for income tax purposes, a businessman can go to Vancouver and as long as he goes to wholesale and says: "How do you do?" and does some business he can charge up his expenses legally, or he can buy a few cross-cut saws or wedges and comply with the law. Or he can go to Toronto and do some business or he can go to New York. Any businessman can do that and enjoy a holiday as long as he does some legitimate business. The point is that he can take a business trip, combine it with a holiday, and properly charge up a considerable amount of the expenses to the operation of his business. There are other cases that I could give as illustrations of the opportunities for deduction. Once again I want to bring this situation at Trail to the attention of the parliamentary assistant because numbers of the employees have written to me. They are anxious that the government give consideration to this question.
I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant whether consideration has been given to allowing deductions in such cases. If so, why has the decision not been favourable?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to get in my four cents' worth. I should like to support the hon. member for St. John's West

in tihe statement he has made with regard to consideration tor some exemptions while students are attending university. I think the cut-off age of 21 is an old formula which has outlived its usefulness. As the hon. member points out, across the country there are many students in universities today who are 25 to 30 years of age. I myself have run into a great many of them. That situation is due to the fact that the government embarked on a program of university education for returned personnel. That is particularly true with regard to dentistry. We are crying to high heaven for doctors. We are importing them for defence industries. I think that consideration should be given to any encouragement which the government can give to students in universities who are taking courses in medicine, engineering or dentistry. I think that cut-off age of 21 should be forgotten and that the formula should be "while attending university".
During the budget debate I raised a point that nobody else has taken up on the resolution. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant whether any consideration was given to the matter of exempting, as a tax offset, the expenses of a person who is obliged to hire a housekeeper. I know that there is already an exemption of $1,000 for the wife; but where she is in ill health or is in an institution the man with a family is obliged to hire a housekeeper. He has to pay her wages. He has to maintain her, and he is up against the responsibility of maintaining his wife in an institution which is pretty costly in this country today. In my remarks on the budget speech I suggested that consideration should be given to permitting as a tax offset the expenditures of a person who is maintaining a home when he has to hire someone to come in and look after that home while his wife is in an institution or is ill at home. Has any thought been given to that matter?

I am not a bachelor, but I would like to put in a word for bachelor farmers who are operating a farm. I understand- in fact I have had complaints-that they are not allowed1 to deduct as a farm expense wages for a housekeeper. That is one of the wrongs that should be righted at this session without any further delay, because, if that farmer took the time himself to do the work that the housekeeper does, it would cost him far more to pay the worker on the farm to carry on the work that he would do if he were not doing the work that the housekeeper would do.
I have listened to the hon. member for St. John's West and to the hon. member for Cape Breton South and many others speak
Income Tax Act
on further exemptions for those attending colleges and such institutions. I think that exemption should be granted also.
There are programs undertaken by the government, and many of the students who are carrying on are not able to do justice to their studies because of the hardships brought about by financial difficulties.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If I can recall the series of questions, the first one had to do with university students. As far as they are concerned, we have already had some discussion on it. I think the point was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. It is a problem which is raised each year by correspondence either from parents or from members of parliament. The answer is neither a simple nor an easy one. It is again this matter of trying to do indirectly what is better done directly. The best way to handle it for university students is by bursaries or loans. Indirectly they are tax relief. When we exempt them from that tax relief again it is a matter of whether it is fair or whether it is progressive. After all, it has long been recognized that a person of 21 should be self-supporting-I am quite sure that the hon. member for Cape Breton South was earning his living long before he was 21-and if the family circumstances are such that the breadwinner of the family can support him when he wants to go on further to university, they are in much better financial circumstances than other families who may have equally deserving boys who, because they have not that financial support, must go out to work, as many members of this house have had to do, to finance their university careers. Therefore the first element of injustice creeps in. The less wealthy, who cannot support their boys, are going to get no tax relief.
The second point, of course, is that in such cases when a son who is a man is supported by his father to get a university education as a dentist, a doctor or an engineer, he is making a pretty large investment in his future. I would say that the recovery is made in most cases by the son paying back when he is finished and has got the better class of employment he has obtained as a result of that investment by his father. I do not think very many think they should repay their parents the cost of education provided when they were children; but certainly when an adult man is supported by his parents at university or a professional school I would imagine the recompense would come from the man himself when he is out earning his living in that chosen profession.

Income Tax Act
The third point of course is, again, where are we going to draw the line? People have mentioned universities. Well, if we keep it strictly to universities then the example given by the hon. member for St. John's West does not apply. He used the example of a boy going to a conservatory. Is a conservatory a university? Then there are boys who go to schools, such as vocational schools here and in the United States, at the age of 21, 22 and 23. Generally they work and save to go to these vocational schools. Could they be classed as universities? The reason for the present attitude is the objection first of all that this is another case of trying to do indirectly in a minor way through tax relief things which should be done much better directly through bursaries or loans at the universities.
The next point was the matter of transportation for the workers. That again is a matter of one of those ordinary expenses which are embodied in the ordinary living costs of everyone. Unusual transportation expenses might be in the same class as unusual medical expenses; but in this case, especially with those workers who are in a bargaining position because they are highly organized in the plant to which the hon. member referred, if they have to travel this long distance to work, they know in their own minds that that is a cost of living to them and they bargain accordingly directly with the employer for a wage to compensate for that.
The hon. member referred to the fact that the individual businessman is allowed1 the cost of expenses of making business trips. I think he mentioned hardware particularly. I am not much of an expert on that; but again there is a great difference between a business operation and a salary or wage job. In securing a salary or a wage the workers must have in mind the cost of the ordinary or usual expenses, of food and clothing, transportation, ordinary medical expenses and the like, exemption for which is given in our basic allowance.
The other point was made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. That is the matter of medical expenses. Quite a bit is done in this respect. In connection with the example of the widower who has to hire a housekeeper because he has dependent children, he has the right to claim married status as far as the income tax exemption is concerned. If on the other hand he has to have a housekeeper because his wife is at home bedridden and needs attendance the year round, then that could be claimed under the medical exemption class as part of
[Mr. Sinclair J	_____
his medical expenses. There is not as yet any provision for the other case he mentioned, namely, that of a man who requires to hire a housekeeper to take care of his house and children because his wife is a patient in an institution. His housekeeper then is not in attendance on the wife. However, that matter can be given consideration.
The last question is a most interesting one, namely, that of bachelor farmers. I might point out that our income tax rates are heavily weighted against bachelors in every respect, again on this very sound principle which has been enunciated earlier by hon. members that the income tax is the fairest and best tax because it is based on ability to pay and because it can be made progressive. Well, certainly, bachelors have a much greater ability to pay than men who have wives and are raising and supporting children. The second thing is that actually through taxes we are able to achieve or at least to encourage desirable ends, and I think as far as this country is concerned it is desirable that most of the bachelors settle down to a happy married life and make sure that this country is going to go on and expand in numbers. And if that measure of encouragement is given by the present taxation system I think it is a matter of general acceptance.
Perhaps these bachelor farmers in the end will marry their housekeepers and enjoy the benefits, both socially and through the tax return, of marriage.

I just want to say a word about this matter of extending the exemptions for students who are attending university. I was very much impressed with what the parliamentary assistant had to say. I followed it with keen interest. Perhaps he had some good arguments. I wish to support the contention of the hon. member for St. John's West, and others, that this age limit of 21 should be raised, particularly for students who are attending university. Things are different today from what they were when "Clarie" Gillis was a boy, and quite different from what they were when I was a boy.
That was a long time ago.

Very likely. But the young people in that day did not require the standard of education required today to be able to enter into the employment that would earn them a living. Every year since then- every five years, at any rate-the requirements have risen. That is, we are competing more in each five-year period.
The courses are longer.

Yes, and there is greater competition for the jobs that do exist. That has

been proved, I think, by the fact that universities and schools across the country have increased the prerequisites, as well as the length of the courses. That fact in itself indicates that there has been quite a change since "Clarie" was a boy.
Today boys and girls complete their high school education at the ages of 18 or 19 years. They just get nicely started at university, and suddenly their parents are cut off from income tax exemption in respect of those children. The parents have to bear the extra tax as well as the cost of giving these young people the last year or two of their education. I believe the people of this country would wholeheartedly support the Minister of Finance in increasing the age, let us say, to 23 or 24, if they are going to university or college, or to some other training institution in order to complete the education begun before reaching the age of 21, in an effort to make themselves self-supporting.
There was one thing the minister did not say, and that was this, that, when boys and girls are encouraged to go on to higher education, if the Minister of Finance would give this further help to the parents so that these young people might become qualified through their education to earn higher salaries, the minister would get back, in higher returns these boys and girls would be able to earn, anything he might allow.
That is a long-range view.

They would be in a higher tax bracket. We have to look at these things from the long-range viewpoint. 1 appeal to the parliamentary assistant to take into serious consideration the raising of the age limit to 23 or 24, if these people are going to university or to some other training institution to complete education begun before reaching the age of 21. If that sort of cutoff is arranged, I do not think anyone could take exception to it.
Resolution stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stated yesterday that some arrangement had been entered into which we hoped would be satisfactory for the disposal of the surplus meat which is coming on to the market in Canada at the present time. The announcement I am about to make is that there has been agreement among Britain, New Zealand and ourselves. I am about to read the announcement to the house now. This is the statement regarding the meat agreement with Great Britain and New Zealand:
As a result of an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan, Canadian livestock and meat which would normally be sold in the United States are not permitted entry to that market. Canada has therefore a surplus of beef and pork.
Agreement has been reached between the governments of the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Canada whereby Canadian meat will be shipped to the United Kingdom in exchange for New Zealand beef and pork which will in turn be sold through normal commercial channels in the United States. The Canadian meat to be shipped to Britain will not come from or through the affected area in Canada.
The United Kingdom will pay New Zealand in sterling at the existing New Zealand-United Kingdom contract rates and Canada will receive the proceeds from the sale of the New Zealand produce in the United States. As the New Zealand meat has to be exported frozen it will realize less in the United States than would have been received from the fresh Canadian product. Although there will be a net loss to Canada, Canada has expressed a willingness to recompense New Zealand for the trouble involved in implementing the exchange and the determination of a share for New Zealand in any excess there might be of net United States over sterling proceeds is under consideration.
That is the announcement as it is being made in the three countries.
I am sure the house will support me when I say that we greatly appreciate the helpfulness of the governments of Great Britain and New Zealand in making this arrangement possible. While we have naturally not asked them to bear any share of the cost, we do recognize that the arrangement has, to a degree, upset their normal plans for meat delivery. We hope that the British people will receive some compensation through earlier delivery and perhaps also by obtaining larger quantities of meat than might otherwise be possible.
May I also express a word of appreciation of the efforts of our own officers who helped to negotiate the arrangement and of the trade

Trade-Beef and Pork
commissioner service of the Department of Trade and Commerce which has been most helpful at every stage. I can assure the house that there has been the best of co-operation among all concerned, both in Canada, Great Britain and New Zealand, as well as with our friends in the United States.
In addition to the announcement I have just made, which has also been released in Great Britain and New Zealand, I am glad to be able to tell the house that we have today started moving quantities of beef to Montreal for early delivery to Britain. In other words, the meat is already moving. Freezer space on ships has been booked, and there is every indication that the movement can continue without interruption in so far as shipping and other facilities are concerned.
As is well known to members of the house, we have appealed to farmers to hold their cattle off the market in so far as they possibly could in order that the supply of beef might not greatly exceed the Canadian demand. That they have done so is proven by the fact that cattle marketings for the first eighteen weeks of this year are some 25 per cent below those of a year ago. However, in spite of decreased marketings the beef supply has been somewhat in excess of Canadian demand and considerable quantities have been accumulated in storage. It is because of this fact that it is now possible for us to have beef moving to seaboard for early delivery to Britain. As the program continues we have every reason to expect that our markets will be relieved of surplus beef.
I should like to emphasize, however, that it is still highly desirable for farmers who have grass and feed to hold lightweight and unfinished cattle rather than deliver them to the markets. If this is done we are confident that the floor prices can be maintained until the present emergency is past.

Could we have an explanation by the sponsor?

The purpose of this bill is to amend the original act of incorporation of this body, which was carried out by dominion statute in 1909. The first change proposed is to move the location of the head office from Strathcona to Edmonton. At one time Strath-cona was bigger than Edmonton, but it finally became incorporated into Edmonton; just as at one time Calgary thought it was a bigger city than Edmonton, and the time is coming when it will be incorporated into Edmonton.
Or vice versa.

I wish to assure the hon. member for Calgary West that we are not very fussy about having Calgarians in Edmonton, anyway; but that is the situation. The next important change is to increase the number of elders, the governing body of this church, from three to five. The next change is to increase the value of the real estate that may be held in Canada from some $50,000 to $500,000. Since the incorporation of this body in 1909 the number of members and adherents and churches has continued to grow, making it necessary to hold more real property and to expand the governing body.
I would like to give a very brief historical outline of this church. It claims to be the oldest Protestant church in the world and to have as its founder John Huss, who was burned at the stake in 1415. It takes its name from Moravia, which is a province of what is now Czechoslovakia. The church is noted for

its missionary work and was one of the first to have foreign missions in Labrador and Alaska. There are in my constituency a number of people who belong to this church, and I can assure hon. members that they are good Christians and good Canadians. I think this bill should be referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.
I would like the hon. member to understand that I am quite in accord with this bill, but why is the change being made from one minor city to another in western Canada?
I am not sure that I understand the question. Why is the change being made from what?

As I understand it, the headquarters of this church are being changed from one city to another within the same province, which is more or less a subsidiary of British Columbia. Why is the change being made?

There is no longer a city called Strathcona. It is now the city of Edmonton, which includes what was formerly Stratchona. If my good friend will visit Edmonton, as he should, he will find that it has expanded greatly and, as I said a moment ago, it may eventually take in Calgary.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 6, 1952, consideration in committee of Bill No. 62, to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation-Mr. Larson-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, this is a bill to incorporate a pipe line company to be known as Boundary Pipeline Corporation. The plan of the sponsors of the bill is to pipe natural gas from the province of Alberta to Winnipeg, and thence in due course to the central states of the United States, I presume having in mind more particularly such centres as Minneapolis and St. Paul and possibly Chicago. The applicants as set out in the bill are all described as residents of Regina, but behind them is a United States pipe line engineering firm known as the Fish Engineering Corporation of Houston, Texas.
Your Honour will remember that there was no debate on the second reading of this bill. It got through that stage, perhaps through the negligence of some of the members of the house, with no debate at all,
Boundary Pipeline Corporation and was referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. This evening I wish to comment on one incident which took place while this bill was before the standing committee.
The main witness called on behalf of the applicants for a charter was a certain Robert R. Herring, of Houston, Texas, who is an engineer for this Fish Engineering Corporation. He was being questioned by the member for Calgary West who, without any question, is an authority on oil and natural gas matters. Before that member had finished his examination, some of the government members of the committee intervened and moved the following motion which will be found on page 73 of the proceedings of the committee. It reads:
. . . that sufficient evidence has been obtained for the committee to decide as to the economic practicability of the pipe line under consideration; and that the question be put on the preamble without further examination of the witness. After discussion and the question having been put on the said motion, it was agreed to on the following division:
There follows a list of the names of the members who voted for and against that closure motion. All the Liberal members present at the time voted for that motion, with the exception of the member for Hastings South who voted with the representatives of the opposition parties; for that stand I am glad to give him credit.
I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that the member for Calgary West had not yet finished his examination, and that the passing of that motion also had the effect of preventing other members of the committee from carrying on an examination; each one of them had the right to question the witness. Again, I would point out that this was a private bill and supposedly not sponsored by the government. There was plenty of time available because we were not halfway through that particular sitting at the time this motion was brought forward. We could have sat again in the afternoon. There was absolutely no time to be gained by shutting off the hearing of evidence in that manner. There were no other bills before the committee except this pipe line bill. The result of this motion, of course, was that the bill could not be given full consideration in the committee, because Mr. Herring was the principal witness.
I would point out to Your Honour, and to the members of this house, that actions such as this by a government majority on a committee are unfair, they are unwise and they are contemptuous of the democratic procedure. In fact, they are against the best traditions of this House of Commons. I regret very much that such a stand should be taken by government members in any committee. They would not dare to do it in the house because of the adverse publicity that would

Boundary Pipeline Corporation be at once spread across the country. Yet it was done in a committee, and it is becoming a habit which has got to be stopped. This is one more example of the weakness of this present parliament in that it has such an overwhelming government majority. I would suggest to the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet that they remind their followers that Canada still belongs to the Canadian people and not to the so-called Liberal party.
This bill raises the question of what is to become of the natural gas piped east from the province of Alberta. It is admitted by all concerned that there will be only one line to the east, just as there is to be but one line to the west. I would remind hon. members of the debates which have taken place in this house concerning the question of piping natural gas from Alberta to the west coast. In the fall session of 1949 we had a debate concerning the bills of two groups of applicants who sought to gain charters to enable them to pipe that gas from southern Alberta down into the state of Washington at the first convenient point, and from Washington to the state of Oregon with a branch line up to Vancouver and possibly another branch line up to the Canadian city of Trail. These private bills were talked out in 1949. They were re-introduced in the session of 1950 and, after considerable debate, were finally allowed to go through. The names of the two companies then granted a charter were the Alberta Natural Gas Company and Prairie Transmission Lines Limited. It is significant that the Fish Engineering Corporation, which is behind the bill we are now considering to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation, was also behind the Prairie Transmission Lines Limited. Last year, in the spring session of 1951, a private bill was introduced which would have incorporated a pipe line company known as Border Pipeline Corporation. The sponsors of this bill also planned to pipe gas or oil, I forget now which it was, to the Pacific coast via the United States. That bill was talked out during that session.
In due course the various companies which had obtained charters applied to the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board for permission to pipe gas from that province. In the month of March of this year a decision was handed down by the board authorizing a company known as West-coast Transmission Company Limited to pipe gas to the west coast from the Peace river district. This meant, of course, that they would pipe it through British Columbia first and then any surplus would go down to the states of Washington and Oregon. Of course, that was the route which we had advocated

throughout, or alternatively the route from Edmonton through the Yellowhead pass and so to Vancouver.
The board having handed down its decision, the Alberta government put through a bill granting permission for the exportation of this gas from the Peace river down to the western Canadian coast. The British Columbia government is, of course, willing to take whatever steps are necessary to assist in the construction of that line, because the legislature of British Columbia has repeatedly taken a unanimous stand in favour of a gas line to the west coast which served Canada before reaching into the United States. The company building this line to the west coast still will need the approval of the board of transport commissioners and of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the latter permission being required to export to the United States. They will also need the permission of the federal power commission of the United States for such export.
It is interesting to note that with respect to this same Fish Engineering Corporation, which is behind the present bill, that when their company, Prairie Transmission Lines Limited, lost out in the race to get permission to pipe gas west, the president of the company at once announced that he was going to rush natural gas into the states of Oregon and Washington from Texas, and in that way prevent the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited from getting Canadian gas into those two states.
As to the export east of gas from Alberta, the Alberta board refused to give any direction for such export. It appears that in that province the exportation of gas is a hot political issue with the Liberals and, I think, the C.C.F. taking the position that no gas whatever should be exported from Alberta, while the Social Credit party has stood for such export. However, it is expected that permission will be granted later this year for the export of natural gas east from the province of Alberta. Hence the question of where that gas is to go is extremely important at the present time.
There are two possibilities. The first is that it will go across the prairie to Winnipeg, then south to Minnesota and other United States centres and possibly to Chicago. The second is that it will go to Winnipeg, then to Fort William, Port Arthur, Toronto, Montreal and possibly the city of Quebec, serving many Ontario and Quebec centres en route.
There have been two companies which have been active in preparing to pipe natural gas east from Alberta. One of them is Western Pipe Lines which was granted a charter in

the rush just before the election of 1949, before any of us except the Minister of Trade and Commerce understood what all this pipe line excitement was about. The other is Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited which was incorporated in 1951. The first of these companies, namely Western Pipe Lines, plans to follow the United States route, to Winnipeg and then down into the United States. The second one, namely Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, plans to build the all-Canadian route. Both of them have spent several million dollars in making surveys of the respective routes, of the centres that will be served, and also in developing reserves of gas in the province of Alberta.
The applicants for this present charter now come along, and they have done practically no development work whatever. They have made no extensive surveys. They are trying to cash in on the efforts of these other companies. Their expenditures amount to $25,000. I asked that question in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Hon. members will find this at page 11 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee:
By Mr. Green:
Q. There is one other question I would like to ask you, Mr. MacTavish.
I may say that Mr. MacTavish is parliamentary agent of the applicants for this charter. The question continues:
How much money has been spent by the applicants to date in connection with this project? A. I think I can find that out for you immediately. X am instructed that about $25,000 has been spent.
They plan a very small pipe to Winnipeg, namely a 16-inch pipe, whereas Western Pipe Lines are planning a 24-inch pipe and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited a 30-inch pipe. It was admitted, in effect, by Mr. Herring in the committee that all his people are trying to do is to get their toe in the door in Alberta; that is, to get a charter and get permission to put in this small pipe line and in that way get their toe in the door. In that way they would be in a preferred position because there is to be only one pipe line to the east.
Then in the committee they admitted that they plan eventually to pipe gas to the United States. At page 63 of the proceedings of the committee, in my examination of Mr. Herring, are to be found the following question and answer:
Q. Now, in this bill which you are sponsoring, which you are supporting, you are laying another plan to get Alberta gas down into the central states? A. That is correct.
They admit that they have no intention whatever of building to Ontario or Quebec. I would point out to hon. members that in
Boundary Pipeline Corporation section 6 of the bill we find that the applicants are asking power to build within the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, or outside Canada. There is no mention whatever of Ontario or Quebec. We asked that question also in the committee of Mr. MacTavish. It will be found at page 7 of the proceedings. The question is:
Q. Mr. Chairman, arising out of the question just asked by Mr. Mclvor,-
I am hoping that the hon. member for Fort William will follow my remarks tonight because I shall try to set him straight on the views he expressed the other night.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I am following the hon. member.

The question continues:
-as I read the bill you are not asking any power to build a pipe line in the province of Ontario at all. Is that correct? You are only asking to build in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba or outside Canada, so that obviously, it is not the intention of this company to build a pipe line in the provinces of Ontario or Quebec. Is that correct? A. That is correct, sir.
Here I should like to refer to the statement made on Tuesday evening in this house by the hon. member for Fort William. It will be found at page 1930 of Hansard. He spoke in favour of this bill, if you please, and he said:
I object vigorously to any measure providing for a pipe line that will come to Winnipeg but will not come to Fort William and Port Arthur.
Of course the one way to prevent Fort William from getting gas is to have this present company given permission to go ahead. The hon. member continues:
I supported this bill-
It stops at Winnipeg.

-because the amendment I moved was carried. The purpose of my amendment was to eliminate the words "outside Canada" . . .
I now turn to page 74 of the proceedings of the committee. It so happens that the hon. gentleman did not move an amendment to strike out the words "outside Canada". That amendment was moved by the hon. member for Calgary West and the hon. member for Fort William voted against it. That vote is recorded here at page 74 of the proceedings. I only hope that the hon. member's constituents in Fort William will get the facts a little bit straighter than he did. I would point out further that in a return tabled for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in answer to a question asking whether any cities had requested that the pipe line should be built through Canada, the information is given showing that some had, and they are listed as the township of Nipigon, the corporation of the city of Fort William and the city of Port Arthur.
Mr. Chairman, I had not expected to speak in this connection, but I am glad to note that my hon. friend from New Brunswick is insisting that I do so.
I hope you speak for an hour.

The hon. member for
Maple Creek, in a forty-two minute filibuster, has told us of what a great riding he has. I presume it is as great a district as he has said. He paid me the compliment-perhaps it was not due me-that last year I had led a filibuster in connection with an all-Canadian pipe line. Possibly I am not entitled to all that honour, because that discussion developed as a result of co-operation among a few of us from British Columbia.
Boundary Pipeline Corporation
Those of us who did lead the filibuster are proud of the fact; and we would like the hon. member for Maple Creek-which, I believe, is a small district in Saskatchewan-to know that we are proud of that filibuster. Already in British Columbia, in the municipalities of Richmond, Burnaby and other districts, contracts have been let to a value of $20 million or $30 million to expand the oil services in that province.
When I was home at Easter one of the greatest privileges tendered to me was that of having my picture taken. Like all politicians, even those who opposed the all-Canadian route, I like to have my picture taken. So it was not only a privilege but a pleasure to have that happen.
Near my farm is located the small station of Clayburn. Indeed, the siding is on my farm. I believe all members from British Columbia will know where it is. It was my good fortune to have my picture taken alongside two carloads of 24-inch steel pipe for the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. The pipe was being unloaded at that siding.
We know that large contracts have been let for the expansion of refineries in British Columbia, although they are not located in my riding. But the fact remains that the main line goes right through the centre of Cruickshank's farm, and I got a real kick out of having that picture taken.
That pipe line goes through there because a few of us from British Columbia, despite the majority of members from that province, stated our position. I well recall that an agreement was made in my office, room 565 in this building, at seven-thirty in the evening, that those of us who had taken part in the so-called filibuster would withdraw our objection if it was agreed that the main line would be within Canada. I know those who supported me will agree with what I say in this connection.
I do not know whether all hon. members read the Ottawa Citizen, nor am I sure which party that newspaper supports. However, in its issue of Friday, May 9, there was an editorial with which I agree, and which I believe will receive approval of other hon. members, because it expresses the views of members from British Columbia. It is headed "Intelligent British Columbians" and refers to a Gallup poll. I do not find that any other province is mentioned. And though my father was born in Ontario, I must accept this statement in the Gallup poll which says that British Columbians are the most intelligent people in Canada.

Oh, oh.

Boundary Pipeline Corporation
Well, it is right there in the editorial. That is what the latest Gallup poll says; it is not my statement.
The biggest insult to Canada.
It is the Gallup poll that says that.
The Gallup poll makes mistakes.

It is not my statement, but that of the Gallup poll. And just to satisfy some of my colleagues who surround me, my colleagues from other provinces, let me say again that it was not my statement. However, judging from their stand in connection with an all-Canadian pipe line, when it was discussed at the last session, I doubt whether they would qualify. I do not have to take up the time of the house-
You can have ten minutes more.

But I am sure my colleagues from Ontario and Quebec must be as interested in the development of their provinces and the economy of Canada as we were in the development of British Columbia. It will be noticed that I am not having as many interruptions from British Columbian or other western members as I had last year.
One of my colleagues from British Columbia says-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to address the chair and, so far as possible, to speak to the bill.

I am definitely interested in the bill, because we won last time, and we now have this development out there. We have even had gas granted by Alberta, as will be admitted by the acting leader of the Social Credit party. That gas is going to the town of Trail and, in spite of what was done by the member from Trail, it will cut their costs in half. That is what we are trying to do for eastern Canada.
Pardon me, but did I hear you say, "In spite of the member for Trail"?

Oh, I beg your pardon; I should have said Kimberley, which is a suburb of Trail. We know that Trans Mountain has now let contracts and is actually building an all-Canadian pipe line into British Columbia, a fact of which I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver South is proud. They have made the contract, and they axe building it.
I supported it.
You did not. You supported nothing, so far as an all-Canadian route is concerned.
I supported it by my speech in the house on the pipe line bill sponsored by the hon. member for Vancouver South, for an all-Canadian route for the oil pipe line- not one for the gas.
Any support the hon. member for Kootenay East gave us was after we got the amendment through and not before. Gas is more important than oil to the town of Kimberley from which he comes.
Oh, oh.
The records will show what are the facts, and the people of your riding will read the records too. What we are trying to do-
Talk it out.

-is to ensure that this bill is not passed in order that the resources of Canada may be utilized for the benefit of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and possibly the maritimes. We have no objection whatsoever to any surplus being exported to the United States as in the case of our pulp and anything else, but we believe that primarily our resources should be utilized within our own country. I have heard colleagues who sit not so far away from me advocate this very thing in connection with our great timber resources.
Don't point at me.

Let us utilize our
resources first to build up industry, create employment and provide security for the great labour unions that some members fail to represent at times. Let us build up that security and then send any surplus to the United States, our best neighbour and our best friend in this world next to Great Britain. We believe these resources should be developed primarily for the purpose of building up Canada, with the surplus being exported. That is what we are saying now, and we are rather surprised that members from Ontario and Quebec and even from the maritimes apparently by their silence give approval to the bill when obviously if permission is granted by the province of Alberta and the board of transport commissioners the gas will be exported to the United States. I have only talked for eighteen minutes.
And have not said anything.
Maybe I have not said anything yet but my colleague is afraid to get up and say anything for or against.
Let us have the Gallup poll.
I had better refer to that again.
Order.
Order my eye. Those who are speaking now are not courageous enough to speak on behalf of their own province.
We do not need to have any lessons from the hon. member on anything else but what he is doing now.
If I am out of order I withdraw. The leader of the opposition has come into the chamber, and I should like him to note the editorial in today's Citizen.
He will not like it.
This includes Carleton county as well. According to the latest Gallup poll-
He is not listening.
May I ask the hon. member a question? I should like to ask the hon. member if he thinks the Gallup polls are perfect and never make a mistake?

I do not think they are perfect. I have been asked a direct question, Mr. Chairman, and I would reply that the Gallup poll forecast that the Liberals would be elected at the last election and they were. That is as nearly perfect as they can be. I hope the hon. member for Carleton appreciates the stand taken by some of us from British Columbia. Perhaps I had better read the heading of the editorial again. It is headed, "Intelligent British Columbians". That is what we are. Some of us are naturally modest, but we got a pipe line with an allCanadian route which is under construction today. The right of way is being cleared and the pipe is being unloaded on sidings in Canada in spite of those who wanted an allAmerican route, including some British Columbia members. Apparently some of us qualify for the wording of the headline in spite of those who want to build an allAmerican route. Their remarks fall right off my back. I used to shoot ducks in the Kootenays years ago before some people were born.
You are not shooting ducks now.
You are shooting an owl.

Maybe I am shooting an owl but I shot it last year with the assistance of a few members, not including some of my colleagues. The result is that over 70 cars of steel pipe are being unloaded in the province of British Columbia to build an allCanadian pipe line. It will result in $30 million to $40 million being spent on new refineries in spite of opposition. My friend is very brilliant in some ways but he pulled a boner that time when he bucked the province of
Income Tax Act
British Columbia, western Canada, the economy of all Canada and the unions of Canada by trying to divert gas and oil to the United States before utilization to the fullest extent had been put into effect in Canada. I do not want to take up too much time.
Oh, no.

I have only spoken for some fifteen minutes and I have not read the articles I want to read. However, if this matter comes up at the next session I will read the remarks made on May 5, 1950, by no less an authority than the present Prime Minister of Canada, and I will also read what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. No man in Canada knows more about industry and the development of Canada than the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am going to take a great deal of pleasure next session in putting on the record what he said about the building up of Canada in spite of some of these minor obstacles from western Canada.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being nine o'clock, and the hour devoted to private bills having expired, the house will resume the business under consideration at six o'clock.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

speakerposition: subtopic
Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At six o'clock we were considering the first paragraph of the income tax resolution.

I should like to rise this evening for the main purpose of supporting the request made this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar for an income tax exemption of $3,000 for married people and $1,500 for single persons. The crux_ of these resolutions which parliament is being asked to consider tonight is that income taxes in Canada this year will be higher than ever before in peacetime. In view of the cost of living I feel that it is the people in the lower brackets who are going to be mainly affected. I think the time has come for this parliament, and particularly the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant, to realize that income taxes in Canada have reached the saturation point in peacetime. I think the rates which are proposed in this resolution are going to cause real hardship in this country. After all, you can ask a man to carry a 300-pound load across a room, but if you were to ask that man to carry the same load around a

Income Tax Act
city block you would break his back. That is just what this government is going to do as far as the taxpayers of Canada are concerned.
I believe income taxes in Canada are discouraging initiative. I know farmers in my riding who have come to me and said, "I am going to live in the city this winter. What is the use of my going out raising hogs, raising livestock, working hard throughout the winter, only to give the money to Mr. Abbott?" I know railroaders who have made perhaps twenty trips and then have said, "Thatcher, what is the use of my going out and making any more? I have to give it all to Mr. Abbott." I know businessmen who have said, "What is the use of my trying to go ahead any further? If I do make any more money I just have to give it to Mr. Abbott." So I repeat that in my opinion income taxation in Canada has reached the saturation point.
I was disappointed this afternoon when the chairman ruled that the hon. member for Greenwood could not propose savings. How on earth are we going to get the income tax down unless the government is interested in hearing some suggestions for savings. The hon. member for Greenwood was prepared to make such suggestions this afternoon. A few weeks ago I had the privilege of making a few suggestions. I must say those suggestions were received with some ridicule, perhaps a little contempt and certainly derision. No attempt was made by the minister to answer them in any way. The only one that was answered in the house was by the parliamentary assistant this afternoon. He answered one out of about fifteen which he thought might cause me political embarrassment. That was the only trouble he went to at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I wanted to be in order, so the one I answered was the only suggestion which was relevant to the actual item we were discussing. I would also draw attention to the fact that most of the hon. member's observations are not in order as far as this resolution is concerned. That was the reason the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood in regard to savings were ruled out, not that he should not have the right at the proper time to make whatever observations he wishes on that matter.

I can only assume that this government is not interested in hearing about savings. Perhaps any savings we might suggest would not be reasonable; I do not know. But at least as opposition members we are trying to make a few suggestions, and it seems to me the least the parliamentary assistant should do is make some attempt to analyse

them. Again I say that income taxes in this country are too high, and unless something is done in the next year to get them down we are going to run into trouble.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the discussion terminated on paragraph 1?
Agreed.
